easa.q: Atmospheric pressure is measured with an instrument called a:
easa.explain: A mercury barometer records pressure in inches of mercury (EASA p. 1.2).

easa.q: An aircraft can fly ____ at a high altitude where the air density is low than at a low altitude where the air density is greater.
easa.explain: Fewer particles per unit volume means less resistance (EASA p. 1.4).

easa.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does most civilian aviation take place?
easa.explain: Temperature falls with height in the troposphere, where most civil aviation takes place (EASA p. 1.5).

anderson.q: At a point on the wing of a Boeing 727 the pressure is 1.9×10⁴ N/m² and the temperature 203 K. The air density there (R = 287 J/(kg·K)) is:
anderson.detail: ρ = 1.9×10⁴/(287 × 203) = 1.9×10⁴/58 261 = 0.326 kg/m³. The Solution Manual gives the same 0.326.

anderson.q: In the test section of a supersonic wind tunnel p = 1058 lb/ft² and ρ = 1.23×10⁻³ slug/ft³. The temperature there (R = 1716 ft·lb/(slug·°R)) is:
anderson.detail: T = 1058/2.1107 = 501 °R, about 41 °F or 278 K. Rankine is an absolute scale.

anderson.q: A mercury U-tube manometer connects the wind-tunnel model to the atmosphere (1.01×10⁵ N/m²). The two mercury columns differ by 20 cm, with the high column on the model side. The pressure on the wing is (ρ_Hg = 1.36×10⁴ kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²):
anderson.explain: The higher mercury column sits on the lower-pressure side, so p_model = p_atm − ρgh.
anderson.detail: p = 1.01×10⁵ − (1.36×10⁴)(9.8)(0.2) = 1.01×10⁵ − 26 656 = 74 344 N/m². Matches the 7.43×10⁴ in the Solution Manual. A common slip is adding instead of subtracting.

anderson.q: A Zeppelin of 15 000 m³ and 14 m maximum diameter flies straight and level at 30 m/s at a standard altitude of 1000 m (ρ ≈ 1.112 kg/m³) with C_L = 0.05 (based on maximum cross-section). Its total weight is:
anderson.explain: W = Archimedes buoyancy B + aerodynamic lift L.
anderson.detail: The ISA density at 1000 m is 1.1116 kg/m³. B = ρVg = 1.1116 × 15 000 × 9.8 ≈ 1.634×10⁵ N; q = ½ρV² = 500.2 Pa; S = πd²/4 = 153.9 m²; L = qSC_L = 3850 N; W = B + L ≈ 1.673×10⁵ N. Counting only aerodynamic lift gives 3850 N, which is wrong.

generated.q: At 40 000 ft in ISA, roughly what fraction of the sea-level pressure remains?
generated.explain: Pressure falls exponentially, not linearly; the ISA formula gives 2.72 psi.

generated.q: The ISA temperature at the tropopause (11 000 m) is:
The ISA temperature at 30 000 ft (troposphere) is approximately:
At constant pressure, doubling the absolute temperature makes the density:
generated.explain: ρ = p/(RT): doubling T halves ρ.

generated.q: Why is humid air less dense than dry air at the same p and T?
opts: Water vapour raises the atmospheric pressure
Water vapour is heavier but expands more
A water molecule is lighter than the N₂ and O₂ molecules it replaces
Water vapour raises the air temperature
generated.explain: EASA: water vapour weighs about 5/8 as much as the same volume of dry air.

generated.q: On a hot, humid day at a high-altitude airport, the take-off run is:
opts: shorter because the air is light
generated.explain: Low density reduces lift and thrust; drag falls too but does not compensate.

generated.q: ISA density at 10 000 ft is approximately:
generated.explain: EASA Figure 1-7 gives 0.9; the computation gives 0.905.

generated.q: ISA pressure at 20 000 ft in hPa is approximately:
generated.explain: EASA gives 465.4 hPa; the computation gives 465.6 hPa.

generated.q: ISA temperature at 10 000 ft is approximately:
generated.explain: 15 − 2 × 10 = −5 °C by the −2 °C per 1000 ft rule; EASA gives −4.8 °C.

generated.q: In which layer does temperature increase with altitude (outside the isothermal ISA model)?
generated.explain: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet and warms the air (EASA p. 1.5).

generated.q: At sea level the temperature is 15 °C above ISA (30 °C). The density altitude is approximately:
generated.explain: The real density is below ISA so the aircraft behaves as if higher.

generated.q: According to EASA the troposphere at the equator extends to about:
generated.explain: Over the poles only 25 000–30 000 ft, on average about 38 000 ft.
